opus-5.5.text:
I think the complexity has shifted. A couple of years ago, most of it was in pre-training: scaling the data, the model, and the infrastructure so that a very large run stays stable. That's still hard, but for a genuinely usable agent, a lot of the difficulty now comes from everything around pre-training, and from how the pieces interact.

The first layer is the environment. With a chatbot you train on text and you're mostly done. With an agent, the model has to act: search, write and run code, operate a browser, call tools, work over many steps. So you need a large number of environments that are realistic, diverse, and stable enough to train on at scale. Building those is real engineering. A tool may be flaky, a web page may change, a sandbox may break, and every one of those becomes noise in the training signal. Much of the work is unglamorous infrastructure: simulators, sandboxes, rollout systems that run thousands of long-horizon trajectories in parallel without falling over.

The second layer is reward, or more broadly, how you define what "good" means. For math or coding with unit tests you have verifiable rewards, and that's relatively clean. But a general-purpose agent has to do things like research a question, write a report, or finish a messy multi-step task for a user, where correctness isn't binary. If the reward is slightly wrong, the model is very good at finding the shortcut. It will reward hack. So you spend a lot of effort designing rewards, checking them, and catching the cases where the model learned something you didn't intend.

The third layer is long-horizon credit assignment and efficiency. An agent trajectory might be dozens or hundreds of steps, with a long context full of tool outputs. Training RL on that is expensive and unstable. You have to think about context management, how the model summarizes or forgets, how you handle partial rollouts, and how you keep training throughput high when each sample takes so long to generate. Systems and algorithms become very tightly coupled here. You can't design the RL algorithm without thinking about the infrastructure, and the reverse is true too.

Then there's generalization, which I think is the deepest part. You can't build an environment for every task a user will bring. So the real question is whether the model learns transferable abilities, like planning, reflecting, recovering from errors, and knowing when to use which tool, rather than memorizing particular environments. That depends a lot on the base model's capability, which is why pre-training still matters so much. RL amplifies what's already there. If the base model has strong reasoning and good priors, agentic training generalizes much better.

Finally, "usable" is its own bar. A benchmark score isn't usability. Users care about reliability, latency, cost, whether the model gives up too early or loops forever, and whether it's honest about what it did. Closing the gap between "it can do this in a demo" and "it does this reliably for real people" requires a tight loop between product feedback and training, and that loop is itself a kind of system you have to build.

So if I had to summarize: the complexity isn't in any single component. It's in making pre-training, environments, rewards, RL infrastructure, and product feedback work together as one system, where a weakness in any part shows up as a weakness in the agent.

r001.rationale: The response discusses long trajectories and separately discusses generalization, but does not say that longer action sequences increase the generality required of the model.

r002.rationale: It calls generalization the deepest part, but summarizes system complexity as making several components work together rather than identifying training for generality as the main source.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the complexity is less in any single module and more in how many things have to be good at the same time, and how tightly they interact.

Take the most basic version of an agent: a model that can run a loop with tools over a long horizon. To make that actually usable, you first need long-context that is not just "can read 1M tokens" but can stay coherent across hundreds of tool calls, where its own outputs become the context. Every error it makes is now in the context too, so the model has to be robust to its own earlier mistakes. That's a different property from one-shot QA quality.

Then there is the environment layer. For pre-training you just need data. For an agent you need environments, and environments are much harder to scale. You have to build sandboxes that are realistic, that have reliable reward signals, and that don't let the model exploit the grader. Our experience is that a large fraction of the engineering goes into infrastructure: running tens of thousands of containers, handling rollouts that are long and highly variable in length, making sure a single stuck browser or shell doesn't block the whole training batch. The RL algorithm itself is honestly a smaller part of the work than people assume.

The third piece is the reward. For math and code you have verifiable answers. For general agentic work — writing a research report, operating a website, fixing a repo — the result is partially verifiable at best. So you need a mix: rubric-based judges, outcome checks, self-critique, and you have to keep these from being gamed. Reward hacking is not a theoretical concern; it shows up almost immediately once the model gets strong enough, and you end up in a loop of patching the grader, which itself is a system.

Fourth, and this is easy to underestimate, is the product loop. "Usable" means a real person tolerates it. That involves latency, cost per task, when to ask for clarification versus just proceeding, and how to show intermediate work. Those decisions feed back into training. For example, if you want the agent to be autonomous for long stretches, you have to train it to not stop and ask; but then it has to be much more careful about irreversible actions. That tradeoff is a training-data design question, not just a UI question.

So when I say the main complexity is system-level, I mean: model capability, environment infrastructure, reward design, and product behavior are all coupled, and improving one often breaks assumptions in another. The organizations that will do well are the ones that can iterate across that whole stack quickly, not the ones with the single best model or the single best harness.

r001.rationale: The response says long-horizon agents must stay coherent across hundreds of tool calls, but does not state that longer action sequences increase the generality required of the model.

r002.rationale: The response attributes complexity to coupled model capability, infrastructure, reward design, and product behavior; it does not identify ensuring model generality during training as the main source.

astra-6.text:
I think the main complexity is in closing the loop between the model, the environment, and the training signal. For a language model, you can start with a relatively simple setup: text comes in, you predict the next token. For an agent, the model takes an action, that action changes the environment, and what it observes next depends on what it did. So the training system has to manage that entire interaction.

That creates two closely connected challenges. One is infrastructure: running many environments, handling tool calls, collecting trajectories, and keeping training efficient when some tasks finish quickly and others take a long time. The other is deciding what actually counts as success. If the reward is easy to measure but only loosely related to what the user wants, you can improve the training metric without making the agent more useful.

And these problems become harder over longer tasks. When an agent fails after twenty steps, was the problem its initial plan, one tool call, or its inability to recognize a mistake and recover? You need training signals that help it improve those behaviors.

So I would frame it as a system problem, rather than just a model architecture problem. The environments, the feedback, and the learning algorithm have to work together. That’s what turns a model that can demonstrate an ability into an agent you can reliably give work to.

r001.rationale: The response says longer tasks make failure diagnosis and training signals harder, but does not state that longer action sequences require greater model generality.

r002.rationale: It identifies coordinating the model, environment, and training signal as the main system complexity; it does not identify ensuring model generality during training as the main source.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main complexity is in the interaction between the model, the environment, and the training process. For a general-purpose agent, you’re not just training it to produce a good answer. You’re training it to take actions, observe the consequences, and continue making progress over many steps.

That makes the whole system much more complicated. You need environments where the agent can actually do meaningful work, tools that behave reliably, and a way to evaluate whether it accomplished the task. If a trajectory fails, was it because the model made a bad decision, the tool failed, or the environment was configured incorrectly? Those things can look very similar in the training data, but they require different fixes.

Then there’s the feedback problem. For a short answer, you can often judge the result directly. For a long task, the agent may make an early mistake that only becomes visible much later. You need a training signal that helps it learn from that, without rewarding shortcuts that happen to pass the evaluator.

So I would put a lot of the complexity in building that closed loop: realistic tasks, reliable execution, trustworthy evaluation, and efficient training. The model is central, but getting all those pieces to work together is what turns a model into a usable agent.

r001.rationale: The response describes agents acting and learning over many steps, but does not say that longer action sequences increase the generality required of the model.

r002.rationale: It places the main complexity in coordinating the model, environment, training, execution, and evaluation, rather than specifically in ensuring the model’s generality during training.
